articles.title: Samsung’s Z Fold 8 Ultra is more of the same, but better than ever
articles.summary: It doesn’t quite feel “Ultra,” but it’s a comprehensive improvement on last year’s phone.
articles.body: What makes the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra so Ultra? Samsung’s first foldable with the Ultra name isn’t a souped-up version of the regular Fold 8, as you might expect. Where the Z Fold 8 is squat and wide, the Fold 8 Ultra retains the thin outer screen and square inner panel of the previous Folds. It does have a substantially better triple rear camera system and a slightly larger battery. But with no support for the S Pen stylus and no Privacy Display, it’s not Ultra in the same way as the Galaxy S26 Ultra. But compare it to last year’s Z Fold 7 and the upgrades look more substantial. Samsung has improved the displays, battery, charging, cameras, chipset, and crease. Most of these are only iterative, but taken together the package is impressive. Does that make it Ultra? I don’t know, and it doesn’t really matter. This is a meaningfully more capable phone than last year’s, albeit for $100 more, and it offers something different than its wider new sibling. Samsung will have to hope that’s enough to hold up against whatever Apple has coming with its expected foldable iPhone next month. [Product: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra | https://www.amazon.com/Samsung-Galaxy-Fold8-Violet-Shadow/dp/B0H12DXK8J/?tag=theverge02-20, https://go.skimresources.com/?id=1025X1701640&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.samsung.com%2Fus%2Fsmartphones%2Fgalaxy-z-fold8-ultra%2Fbuy%2Fgalaxy-z-fold8-ultra-256gb-unlocked-sku-sm-f976uzvaxaa%2F, https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fsamsung-galaxy-z-fold8-ultra-256gb-unlocked-graphite%2FJJGRF3T4PZ] Closed, the Z Fold 8 Ultra has a 6.5-inch cover screen that’s taller than most phones but skinnier too; open, there’s an 8-inch flexible display that’s almost square in its aspect ratio.  At a glance, you’d struggle to tell it apart from last year’s Z Fold 7. It’s the same size, shape, and weight, apart from being fractionally thinner at 4.1mm thick when open. The cameras are in the same spot and look just about identical. In fact, the new set of colors — dark grey, cream, purple, and green — is really the only way to differentiate the two generations by sight. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/samsung-galaxy-z-fold-8-ultra-08_f96bbe.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/samsung-galaxy-z-fold-8-ultra-07.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Samsung argues that while the new Z Fold 8 is designed for content consumption, the taller Ultra is more useful for productivity. The extra vertical space helps if you’re trying to cross-reference documents or navigate multiple inboxes. Personally, I’m more likely to use the larger inner screen for watching video, so I would take the Z Fold 8 over this, but I do see the benefits of the larger space. I wrote two whole articles for my food newsletter across a couple of flights using the Z Fold 8 Ultra’s on-screen keyboard, something I would never consider with a regular phone or even the smaller Z Fold 8. Both displays are brighter than before, now with a peak brightness of 3,000 nits, making them easier to use outside. The inner screen benefits further from a new anti-reflective coating and a small resolution bump to 2256 x 2504. Just as importantly, Samsung has reworked the main screen’s innards, incorporating a new titanium alloy film and a flexible titanium plate. These make the foldable screen thinner and more durable — and combined with the anti-reflective coating, they also make the crease harder to see and feel. Head-on, it’s now almost invisible, though still relatively clear when the light catches it at an off angle. Oppo’s solution in the Find N6, which involves using 3D printing to fill surface-level gaps in the hinge, seems more effective at eliminating the crease, but it’s hard to imagine anyone finding this version especially bothersome. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/samsung-galaxy-z-fold-8-ultra-03.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/samsung-galaxy-z-fold-8-ultra-04.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The biggest year-over-year upgrade is the battery. For the first time, Samsung has adopted silicon-carbon battery chemistry, which makes it possible to fit higher-capacity batteries into the same-size space. As a result, the Z Fold 8 Ultra has jumped from a 4,400mAh battery last year to 5,000mAh, despite being fractionally thinner. The phone easily lasts a day, even with a few hours of inner screen use, and I usually have 30 to 40 percent left when I head to bed. The bigger battery has been bolstered by faster charging — 45W wired and 20W wireless — though the phone is still only Qi2 Ready, meaning there are no charging magnets inside, and it requires a Qi2 case to hit top wireless charging speeds. That helps keep it thin, in fairness, so may be a worthy tradeoff. An IP68 rating is another major omission; the IP48 rating here means good water protection but limited guarantees against dust and sand. Samsung removed S Pen support in last year’s Z Fold 7, and it’s still missing here. There’s also no sign of the impressive Privacy Display technology introduced in this year’s S26 Ultra. [Image: Unlike the regular Z Fold 8, you get three rear cameras on this phone. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/samsung-galaxy-z-fold-8-ultra-10.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Then there are the cameras. If you’re picking between the Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra, then form factor aside, this is the only difference that matters. The Ultra gets the same 50-megapixel, f/1.9 ultrawide as the Fold 8, but its 200-megapixel main camera is substantially superior in both detail and light capture. And the presence of a 10-megapixel, 3x telephoto adds a welcome versatility that the regular Fold 8 lacks. It’s far from the best telephoto in any phone — it’s an area where manufacturers like Vivo and Xiaomi have devoted considerable resources, including larger sensors and superior stabilization — but just having the option makes this a more flexible camera. I wouldn’t push the zoom much beyond its 3x optical range though, with significant noise creeping in above 6x or so. There’s an impressive level of consistency between the three lenses in most conditions, though just occasionally the ultrawide comes out a little differently. It’s usually more muted, though at least once, it took the most vivid shot. Low-light performance across all three lenses is good, though they’re all guilty of over-lightening the nighttime sky and creating flare around brighter lights.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/20260731_230211.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Samsung’s software updates this year are relatively slight. There’s My FanCam, a video editing feature that uses AI to crop videos in on a specific person. Google’s Gemini Intelligence task automation is supported, but so far isn’t available in the UK, meaning I haven’t tested it. Now Nudge, Samsung’s take on Pixel Magic Cue, has apparently been updated to suggest helpful contextual actions (like adding an event to your calendar) to carry out in split-screen. In a week of using the phone, I haven’t seen it pop up once, even after subjecting myself to Samsung Keyboard the whole time because some reports suggest that’s a requirement.  [Image: Samsung’s stark and simple design language is still among the best out there. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/samsung-galaxy-z-fold-8-ultra-01.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I’ve been more impressed than I expected by the Z Fold 8 Ultra. I thought it would struggle to compete with recent excellent foldables from Oppo and Honor, but in reality, it’s a fairly close contest — and unlike those phones, it’s actually on sale in the US. Its cameras still aren’t at the level of Oppo and Honor’s, and without an S Pen or a Privacy Display, I’d quibble over how Ultra it all really is. But for those who prefer the tall, square foldable form factor, this is a worthy follow-up to the Z Fold 7. The substantially larger battery alone justifies the $100 price hike.  I don’t know which of Samsung’s two Z Fold 8 phones I’d buy this year — really, I want the Z Fold 8’s form factor with the Ultra’s cameras squeezed in — but that indecision is testament to the fact that you can’t go too far wrong with either. Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge --- Agree to Continue: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, you must agree to: * Google Terms of Service * Google Play Terms of Service * Google Privacy Policy (included in ToS) * Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.” * Samsung End User Licence Agreement * Samsung Privacy Notice * Samsung Terms and Conditions There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including: * Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services * “Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.” * Send usage and diagnostic data to Google * Google Gemini Apps Privacy Notice if you opt in to using Gemini Assistant * Turn on Samsung offline finding * Samsung news and special offers * Samsung personalized advertising * Bixby personal data intelligence * Samsung customization service Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements. Final tally: seven mandatory agreements and more than nine optional agreements. ---

articles.title: Wacom's MovinkPad 11 is a fun, midpriced entry point for digital artists | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The MovinkPad 11 a versatile little graphics tablet that can help make your wildest digital art dreams come true.
articles.body:
Since the advent of the internet, there has been a dedicated digital art community that’s all about creating through computing.

Wacom, a Japanese company founded in 1983, is considered one of the longstanding leaders in this sector. One of the oldest producers of graphics tablets in the world, Wacom has spent the last few years iterating on its MovinkPad series — a specialized Android tablet that creators can use to spin up digital art at the click of a button or the swipe of a stylus.

I’m not a professional artist, or even a hobbyist. But I am a tech enthusiast and was interested to see how a digital art newbie like myself might use a device like the MovinkPad.

Wacom lent TechCrunch a MovinkPad 11 , the first tablet in the series. The MovinkPad 11 is not Wacom’s latest release. That’s the MovinkPad Pro 14 , which came out last fall and costs substantially more at $1100 and offers a number of impressive upgrades, including an OLED screen with 3K resolution and broader color spectrum. But I wanted to start with the first in the series to get to know MovinkPad from its earliest iteration.

The upshot: The MovinkPad 11 is easy to set up and is a capable device that won’t break your budget. At $500, it’s a little too expensive for a casual user who isn’t specifically interested in digital art. But for those who have a passion for digital doodling and not a lot of cash to throw around, it’s a relatively midrange price point — stuck somewhere between budget picks like the Huion Inspiroy H640P (only around $30) and a more high-end item like Wacom’s Cintiq Pro 27 (which is a whopping $3,500 ), or an iPad (up to $1,100).

For those unfamiliar with the digital art community , you might wonder why anyone would ever want to use one of these? If you’re into making art, why not just stick to paper and pencil?

Digital art affords a distinct kind of creative experience that is impossible to replicate anywhere else, proponents argue. Its patrons include graphic designers, cartoonists, animators, and even video game designers. Some traditional artists use tablet art as a sketching and conceptualization method, and then transfer their drawings onto paper. Others do the opposite, sketching something on paper and transferring it to their tablet. Whatever you’re into, the right tablet can go a long way toward helping you realize your creative vision.

The MovinkPad 11 is an 11.45-inch device that comes with 8 gigabytes of memory and 128 gigabytes of storage, and is battery-free, with a USB charger. It weighs just 1.3 pounds, so it’s relatively lightweight and easy to carry around with you wherever you go.

It also comes with the Pro Pen 3, a 6.3-inch stylus that is easy to use and includes three separate side buttons. Those side buttons can be programmed to your liking. Users can also swap out and customize the stylus nibs (Wacom offers a whole variety of $15 replacement nib packs of varying qualities).

I found the stylus to be lightweight, easy to use, and similar to wielding a fine-tipped felt pen.

The tablet was relatively straightforward to set up, although you’ll need to create an initial pin number to log into it. I questioned the reason for this level of security, at least for my sketches. (If you’re worried someone is going to steal your digital drawings, then your device will be locked and protected.) Setting up the pin is easy enough, though — just go to Settings > Security > Privacy. Choose your unlock settings to either swipe or none.

Since it’s an Android device, the MovinkPad can also be synced to your Google account, which could make integrating your creative materials significantly easier.

MovinkPad also comes with its own free digital art software, Wacom Canvas . With Canvas, users have some basic tools that they can use to get their digital sketches up and running. There’s also a paid app, Clip Studio Paint, which offers a larger range of features and capabilities (you can buy a license for a one-time fee that varies by version).

Depending on which program you’re using, the style and functionality of your stylus nib can also be adjusted. Within Clip Studio Paint, for instance, you can choose between a pen, paintbrush, or sketching pencil, and within each of those categories, there are a multitude of options.

The MovinkPad has a long list of competitors — including the iPad, which has its own variety of art apps and a dedicated stylus, the Apple Pencil . However, the MovinkPad offers a more focused and elegant solution than many of those options, and it comes from a longtime player in the graphics tablet space.

If digital art is your thing (or even if it’s not), the MovinkPad 11 is quite a bit of fun. I played around with it for several hours over a recent weekend and managed to work up some pretty goofy drawings. While none of my sketches are destined to hang in the Louvre, it was definitely a fun way to pass an afternoon.

UPDATE Friday, Aug. 14: This story were updated to reflect changes to Wacom’s product prices.

articles.title: Is this $450 laptop from an unknown brand too good to be true?
articles.summary: The Chuwi UniBook is a fairly unknown laptop poised at undercutting the MacBook Neo with an aluminum build, Intel Wildcat Lake chip, and $449 price. But it cuts too much.
articles.body: Finding a good laptop under $500 was hard enough before RAMageddon. They nearly always had cheap hardware and underpowered, often outdated chips. That’s what made the MacBook Neo so disruptive: It offered great build quality and good-enough performance starting at $599. Windows laptops couldn’t touch it. Even though it’s gone up to $699, it’s still the laptop to beat. So when little-known Chinese brand Chuwi announced a $450 Windows laptop with an aluminum build and a brand-new Intel Wildcat Lake processor, it sounded too good to be true. It is. [Product: Chuwi UniBook | https://us.chuwi.com/products/unibook-laptop-intel-core-3-304-series-3-wildcat-lake] The UniBook comes in one configuration: a 14-inch with an Intel Core 3 304 processor, 8GB of soldered RAM, and a user-swappable 256GB SSD. That’s the lowest-end of Intel’s new Wildcat Lake chips, with just five CPU cores: one performance core, and four low-power efficiency cores. And the integrated graphics? A single GPU core. The MacBook Neo’s A18 Pro is a six-core CPU / five-core GPU ensemble, and it’s a hot rod by comparison. --- Component report card * Screen: D * Webcam: D * Keyboard: C * Trackpad: F * Port selection: A * Speakers: F * Number of ugly stickers to remove: 1 --- The UniBook feels sluggish in anything beyond basic web browsing, emails, and messaging. Its benchmark scores confirm how woefully underpowered that chip is. The MacBook Neo trounces it across the board: both single and multicore CPU performance, as well as graphics. Our Adobe Premiere 4K export test took over an hour on the UniBook. (Although at least it didn’t crash out.) I know it isn’t designed for video editing, but neither is the MacBook Neo, and the Neo exports the same video in under 10 minutes. The one edge the UniBook has is a slightly faster SSD. But despite faster storage, the UniBook’s 8GB of RAM is still a hindrance on Windows 11. It didn’t randomly lag like the recent 13-inch Surface Laptop did, but it isn’t hard to overwhelm. As on the 8GB Surface, Windows 11 uses anywhere from 4.6 to over 5GB of memory on the UniBook after a fresh reboot with no additional apps running. Once you open a half dozen Chrome tabs, a couple messaging apps, and a music streaming app, memory usage easily climbs to 7GB.  It’s no surprise Chrome crashed on me a couple times when I pushed it further with over 20 tabs across multiple virtual desktops. This is no problem on Windows laptops with 16GB of RAM, and even the MacBook Neo could handle more before slowing down. And you can count on everything moving like molasses during big file transfers. It couldn’t even load the Start menu or open the calculator app while importing photos into Lightroom Classic until the RAM and SSD bottlenecks eased.  [Image: Simple looks. Frustrating use. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0011.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Even if your computing needs are minimal, the Chuwi’s hardware makes every interaction unpleasant. The screen is washed out, covering just 64 percent of the sRGB color space, and at 300 nits it’s pretty dim. But the worst offender is the trackpad. It’s incredibly stiff to click. You have to press it so hard the whole chassis flexes a little under the pressure. You don’t have to click the trackpad; it can detect taps too, but I never like the loosey-goosey feel of tapping — especially when executing right-clicks or click-and-drags. Using this trackpad made me physically and mentally tired. And clicking around on a laptop? Pretty important! The speakers are an affront to any music you play, as well as anyone else within earshot. They’re a tinny mess. The phone in your pocket has fuller sound. The 720p webcam is only a smidge better, but it’s still offensive to your face (and possibly your self-confidence). It’s almost passable in the best lighting, but it’s low-res, with a green color cast. In dim or backlit lighting you become a dark blur. After a few days, colleagues started greeting me in meetings with, “Oh, you must be on the Chuwi.” It’s like being told “Wow, you look tired.” “Uhh, yeah. Nice to see you too.”  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0006.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0007.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Amid all these downsides, there are a few bright spots. The UniBook does at least have good battery life. It easily lasts up to 10 hours on battery while doing the lightest of work: writing emails, casually browsing the web, and opening the occasional PDF. And the keyboard isn’t bad. It’s backlit, which is a genuine advantage over the MacBook Neo. It’s fine to type on, but the Neo’s and many other Windows keyboards out there feel less spongy. Also, a lack of function lock means adjusting brightness, volume, or media playback always requires a two-key combo. Not a huge deal, but a strange omission of a usual mainstay. The one thing about the UniBook that genuinely surprised me, aside from the initial reverse sticker shock, was its amount of ports. This little thing has five total USB ports, HDMI-out, microSD, and even an ethernet jack. You might expect all that on a massive gaming laptop, not a thin-and-light. But sadly, none of the USBs are faster than 5Gbps, and the HDMI is just 1.4b — topping out at a stuttery 30Hz at 4K. Any money spent on peripherals to offset the Chuwi’s shortcomings would be better spent on a different laptop. I’ve started testing a $500-ish HP OmniBook 3, and coming from the Chuwi, it was a huge relief. Even its cheap-as-they-get Snapdragon X chip offers eight cores, buoyed by twice the RAM and storage of the Chuwi, and that processor already proved it had exceptional battery life when I reviewed it in the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3x.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0008.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0012.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0009.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I wasn’t overly impressed with the Acer Aspire 14 AI, which you can often get around $600, when I pitted it and the IdeaPad against the MacBook Neo, but it’s way better than the Chuwi for $155 more. Its Intel Lunar Lake chip gets good battery life and is powerful enough to play indie games and last-gen 3D titles on ultra-low settings. It has twice the RAM and storage as the Chuwi and nearly as many ports, and the Acer’s ports are much faster. I take no joy in telling you the Chuwi UniBook is bad and frustrating to use. I want to see decent cheap laptops, and I’m all for them coming from lesser-known brands. But Chuwi’s upstart status also brings long-term customer support into question — it doesn’t seem to have US customer service and repair centers like bigger laptop makers. And in early 2026, the company was found to have shipped laptops and mini PCs with older AMD chips disguised as newer, faster ones (even at the BIOS level). Chuwi eventually put out a statement blaming a “production error” and offered refunds for a limited time, but the situation does not inspire confidence. [Image: It’s a shame the UniBook is uniformly bad. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0003.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The UniBook doesn’t leave a great first impression, but I want to remain hopeful that better things are on the horizon — if not for Chuwi, then at least for the Wildcat Lake processor family. Most of the major laptop makers are launching budget laptops with higher-end Wildcat Lake chips to try to compete with the Neo. Microsoft also claims it’s working on improving Windows 11’s performance with 8GB of RAM — which these new laptops desperately need. With laptop prices skyrocketing due to the RAM and storage crunch, we could all use a win. But the UniBook isn’t it. --- Chuwi UniBook specs (as reviewed) * Display: 14-inch 1920 x 1200 60Hz IPS LCD, 300 nits, anti-glare * CPU: Intel Core 3 304 (Wildcat Lake, 5 cores) * GPU: Integrated Intel Graphics * RAM: 8GB LPDDR5 (soldered) * Storage: 256GB M.2 2280 (user-accessible) * Webcam: 720p with physical privacy shutter * Connectivity: Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.2 * Ports: 2x USB-C 3.2 Gen 1 (5Gbps), 2x USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 (5Gbps), 1x USB-A 2.0 (480Mbps), HDMI 1.4b, RJ-45 gigabit ethernet, microSD card slot, 3.5mm audio jack * Biometrics: none (lockscreen password only) * Weight: 2.66 pounds / 1.2kg * Dimensions: 12.38 x 8.7 x 0.65 inches / 314.5 x 221 x 16.4mm * Battery: 53.38Wh (65W USB-C charger included) * Price: $449 --- Photography by Antonio G. articles.title: The Kindle Scribe Colorsoft is a lot of fun, but it’s not a must-have | TechCrunch
articles.summary: While the device is pretty and lightweight, it’s not something the everyday person needs due to its hefty price tag and size.
articles.body:
After testing the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft for two months, I found that it was made for a very specific kind of notetaker and reader. While the device is pretty and lightweight, it’s not something the everyday person needs due to its hefty price tag and size.

However, for those who have been waiting for a color Kindle that doubles as a digital notebook, the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft is worth considering.

The device starts at a steep $630 and is available in two colors: Black and Fig, a pretty purple shade. It weighs just 400 grams and features an 11-inch display that makes it similar in size to a traditional sheet of paper.

Its thin design is impressive, but its larger size means it’s not exactly something you can hold comfortably with one hand. I found it most comfortable to use when it was propped up against my knees while sitting on a bed or placed flat on a desk.

One thing I like about e-readers is that they’re usually quite portable, so I can easily pop one into my purse when I’m on the go. That wasn’t the case with the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft because its size meant I never ended up taking it out of the house. However, if you’re an avid notetaker or researcher, I can see why you’d want to put it in your work bag to take with you to the office or to a coffee shop to get some work done. Beyond those situations, it’s not a device I’d reach for during a quick trip in an Uber or while waiting at a doctor’s office.

The larger size does mean that there’s more room for writing and notetaking, or even sketching or making diagrams. And of course, the larger display makes reading PDFs and other documents easier.

When it comes to reading, the larger screen has both benefits and drawbacks, as the extra space is helpful when reading books with charts or maps, but the size also gets rid of the cozy feeling that makes smaller Kindles appealing.

What I liked about the larger size was that I was able to create an easy-to-read color-coded digital planner and reading journal, especially since the device comes with templates for daily, weekly, and monthly planners. And as someone who normally has a physical reading journal, I found it quite efficient to be able to finish a book and then open up a digital notebook on the same device to log my reading.

The device comes with a Kindle Scribe Pen that attaches magnetically to the side of the e-reader. The pen feels nice in your hand and can be programmed for various actions. The eraser works smoothly and responds almost instantly.

While the color display is fun, it’s important to recognize that colors look more like soft highlighter shades rather than the vibrant tones you see on a regular tablet. That’s not necessarily an issue for notetaking, but it does mean that comics and other visual content won’t look as rich as the original colors.

The device’s color options were useful when highlighting books because I could assign specific colors to different types of notes. For example, while reading a twisty thriller, I used blue to mark details I thought I might need to remember later and red for quotes I enjoyed and wanted to note. It’s also easy to quickly switch between the different colors thanks to the device’s fast refresh rate.

As for battery life, I found it to be excellent. I only had to charge the device twice over the course of two months. It is worth noting, however, that writing uses more power than reading.

All in all, the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft makes the most sense for students, researchers, and journalers who want one device for reading, annotating, and organizing handwritten notes. For everyone else, the steep cost is hard to justify.

If you’re simply looking to upgrade an older Kindle, I don’t think the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft is worth the investment, as you’d be better off with the more reasonably priced Kindle Paperwhite , which starts at $159.99.

articles.title: Zuck’s yacht could have helped a vessel in need but didn’t
articles.summary: The small cruise ship Wilderness Legacy rescued a skiff that ran out of fuel even though Mark Zuckerberg’s yacht was closer.
articles.body: Earlier this week, the Alaskan cruise ship Wilderness Legacy rescued a small skiff stranded near Farragut Bay after running out of fuel. But, according to tracking data reviewed by the Alaska Beacon and Halifax Shipping News, the closest vessel was actually Mark Zuckerberg’s super yacht, Launchpad. Michael Love, a passenger on the Wilderness Legacy, posted on Bluesky that the captain announced the Launchpad was closer, but “repeatedly refused to respond,” which was met with booing from the passengers. The AIS tracking (embedded below) seems to support that the Launchpad was closer to the vessel in trouble, but then stopped near the entrance of the bay. The Wilderness Legacy can be seen passing Launchpad, then turning around and towing the stranded boat back to safety. [Media: https://youtu.be/NTu4gNlK1aE] The US Coast Guard and the Marine Exchange of Alaska did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But Coast Guard Public Affairs Specialist Shannon Shepard told the Alaska Beacon that “at approximately 9:56 p.m., the Coast Guard determined they were not in distress and issued a marine assistance request broadcast on their behalf.” Brian Baker, spokesperson for Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan, told The Verge that “Mark and his family were not on board at the time of the incident. As the Coast Guard noted, the boat was not in distress, and by the time the crew reviewed the Coast Guard contact on a different radio channel from the one they were operating on, the assist was already underway. We’re grateful all parties are safe.”

articles.title: This great retro-inspired keyboard now comes preassembled
articles.summary: The Classic-TKL is one of my favorite keyboard kits, and now you don’t have to build it yourself
articles.body: You probably know just by looking at it if the Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is for you. Do you want a retro-looking wired keyboard without a number pad? Great. Do you care that it doesn’t have wireless? Perfect. Do you want it preassembled? Buddy, you’re in the right place.  But Nathan, you might say, preassembled is the regular way to buy a keyboard. That is the baseline expectation. Most people buying a cake expect a cake, not a box of cake mix. And that’s true, for most people and most keyboards. But until now, the Classic-TKL has only been available as a bare-bones kit, and now you can buy one ready to go, with quality components, for less than the price of doing a similar build yourself.  If you’re like me, figuring out what keycaps, switches, and stabilizers to use, then putting them all together, is a big part of the fun of mechanical keyboards. But if you just want something to type with that looks retro and sounds and feels nice, without having to build it yourself — or if you were going to use classic beige keycaps anyway — then the Underscore Edition might be up your alley.  [Product: NovelKeys Classic-TKL Underscore Edition | https://novelkeys.com/pages/classic-tkl-underscore] The $189 NovelKeys Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is a wired-only, gasket-mounted tenkeyless mechanical keyboard. It has an injection-molded plastic case with a high forehead, reminiscent of the 18-year-old Realforce 86U, and a silicone mat on the base for sound dampening. It also has hot-swap MX switches, full RGB backlighting, and a light bar (both of which can be turned off), and it’s fully programmable using the Via web app.  The Classic-TKL has been around for a couple of years in kit form. I built one and wrote about it in 2024; I also tested the glow-in-the-dark version. I like them a lot! But apparently not everyone who wants a nice retro-looking keyboard also wants a craft project. Michael Sickler, who owns NovelKeys, told me that the Underscore Edition is aimed at giving NovelKeys’ keyboard enthusiast customer base something they can recommend to friends and family. It’s also aimed at professionals who might lurk on the keyboard subreddits and Discords enough to know what they want, but don’t want to build it themselves. (This is basically the same thing Ryan Norbauer told me about his Seneca, except the Seneca is 20 times more expensive.)   [Image: From the top: boulder, lichen, and clay. I tested the clay but look at that green. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/classic-tkl_colors.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The Underscore Edition comes in clay (warm beige), boulder (taupe-ish), and lichen (a dusty green). My review unit is clay, but I’d buy the lichen personally. It ships with NovelKeys’ own Classic Blue switches, GMK CYL Classic Beige keycaps, a USB A-to-C cable, and preinstalled and pretuned TypePlus stabilizers. These are name-brand parts. GMK CYL keycaps are the benchmark for doubleshot Cherry-profile keycaps. They’re several steps in quality above the keycaps that come with a Keychron, for example. The letters and numbers are crisp and clear and the consistency is unmatched. They’re also expensive; you’d pay at least $120 if you bought them on their own, though you would get more keycaps. The Classic-TKL comes with just the ones you need to cover the board. [Image: Nice thick doubleshot keycaps and smooth switches. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268660_Classic-TKL_keyboard_AKrales_0110.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The TypePlus stabilizers are also a good choice; I’ve installed and tuned a couple sets myself, but the people who made them do a better job. There’s no rattle or tick on any of the stabilized keys. And the Classic Blue linear switches (also made by TypePlus) are also nice. They’re smooth and stable, with almost no wobble; at 53g actuation force and 63g bottom-out, they’re medium-heavy, like a lighter version of the Cherry MX Blacks in my first-ever mechanical keyboard in 2009. They’re not silent, but they’re also not as loud as you’d expect a keyboard this beige to be. (I still feel like a blue switch should be clicky, though.)  I try to avoid the “fans of the genre” review. You know, “if this is the kind of thing you like, you’re going to like it.” But once you get past the strictly utilitarian, pretty much everything about mechanical keyboards comes down to preference and taste.  The Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is a well-executed version of what it is. If you want an earth-tone retro-looking tenkeyless board — a classic TKL, if you will — with linear switches and beige Cherry-profile keycaps, it’s a great choice.  [Image: It has a nice side profile. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268660_Classic-TKL_keyboard_AKrales_0169.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] When you think of it as a high-quality preassembled version of an enthusiast DIY keyboard, with name-brand parts, it’s also a good deal. I built the DIY version of the same board with the same stabilizers and similarly priced keycaps in September 2024. It worked out to $276, and took me an hour to put together (most of which was spent lubing and tuning the stabilizers). The Underscore Edition costs $189, $100 more than the bare-bones kit. You can’t get keycaps, switches, and stabilizers of this quality for $100 combined. But it’s also true that $189 can get you a lot of keyboard these days, especially if you’re not attached to the Classic-TKL’s particular vibe.  Even within the tenkeyless form factor, the Evoworks Evo80 costs $169 and comes with an aluminum case and both Bluetooth and 2.4GHz wireless. Same for the $179 Wobkey Crush 80. But those are different keyboards, with different aesthetics. The 8BitDo Retro 87 is closer, with several classic-computing-inspired flavors including Commodore 64 and IBM Model M, for around $100. But — no disrespect to the 8BitDo here — those look maybe a smidge more casual than the Classic-TKL. I prefer the Classic-TKL’s plastic chassis to the aluminum of the Evoworks or Wobkey boards. But I wouldn’t mind if it had wireless. It’d also be nice if it shipped with a few extra keycaps, in case you want Mac legends or Control in its proper place (Caps Lock). While I’m being picky: I also wish it came with the option for MTNU Classic Beige keycaps, rather than just CYL, because I like MTNU better. An electrocapacitive switch option would be nice too, but now I’m just getting greedy. (Actually, now I’m just reinventing the Realforce.)  If you want the Classic-TKL in a different color, or with different switches or keycaps, there’s still the kit version and the Glo version. And if you want a different keyboard entirely, well, those abound. The Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is the thing that it is, and it’s good at that.  I’d still go for the green one, though. Photography by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge except where noted.

articles.title: Clicks' Power Keyboard brings BlackBerry-style typing to any phone — with some compromises | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Clicks’ $99 Power Keyboard brings a customizable, slide-out physical keyboard to MagSafe and Qi2 smartphones, but its added heft can make larger phones awkward to use.
articles.body:
Clicks Technology , the startup determined to bring back physical keyboards to smartphones, began shipping its now-$99 MagSafe-compatible Power Keyboard this summer, after some delays . As of last week, 75% of the preorders from the first batch had shipped to customers.

Designed to work with a range of devices, this new slide-out keyboard with tactile buttons can accommodate different phone sizes and can be used in either portrait or landscape mode, the company says, giving any phone a BlackBerry-like feel.

The device is something of a teaser for what’s to come when Clicks ships its first smartphone, the BlackBerry-like Clicks Communicator , also featuring a physical keyboard, later this year.

Like the upcoming smartphone, the idea behind the Power Keyboard is to provide an alternative to onscreen keyboards for those who miss the speed and reliability that came with typing on a small, physical keyboard.

However, in its current implementation, the Power Keyboard suffers from the same fate as the company’s earlier Clicks keyboard — a smartphone case that included a physical keyboard. It can make the phone feel top-heavy and difficult to hold in portrait mode, especially if you’re using a larger smartphone as I did in tests with the iPhone 17 Pro Max and Pixel 10 XL.

Still, the device itself is crafted with care and could appeal to those who still desperately long for their BlackBerry.

Unboxing the device, we noticed the Power Keyboard was nicely packaged as a premium device would be, with peel-away cling films to prevent scratches during shipping and a full-color Quick Start guide to using the product.

You may first need to charge the device’s battery via USB-C, though we found ours shipped with a charge already. To pair the device with your phone over Bluetooth, press and hold the power button and slide out the keyboard.

We quickly paired the device with our Android phone. We ran into trouble once we switched over to the iPhone. Even after “forgetting” the device on Android, it still refused to pair with our iPhone. Returning to the instructions, it appears this was our mistake. The trick is to press a number key alongside the power button on the keyboard to add a second Bluetooth device. (The only way to actually “forget” a device is by removing it from its slot using the Clicks mobile app.)

The keyboard attaches to your phone via MagSafe or Qi2. If your phone doesn’t support either technology, you could opt to use an adhesive ring or a phone case that adds the magnetic power profile instead.

Once your device is connected, you can then pull the keyboard out when you need to type. Helpfully, the keyboard adjusts to different phone sizes, so it will work with standard models as well as larger Ultra or Pro Max devices. We appreciated the satisfying clicks as the keyboard locked into place on the various sliders. The keyboard offers an adjustable LED backlight, so you can type in the dark.

The keys themselves have a nice, clicky feel and are well-placed, making them easy to reach. While it takes quite a bit of adjustment after years of on-screen keyboards to return to pressing buttons, the learning curve is less steep than it was on the earlier Clicks keyboard case. It’s clear that the company has been iterating on what it learned with its older device, and those lessons have been channeled into this product.

In addition, while Clicks’ older keyboard case pulled power from the phone by way of its USB-C connection, the Power Keyboard instead includes a built-in 2,150 mAh battery.

The product itself has a slimmer profile than some snap-on battery packs, at 119.7 × 76.6 × 15.2 mm, and it doesn’t add an unreasonable amount of weight at 180 grams. Nevertheless, this is not something that would fit well in a woman’s pants pocket. The keyboard could get caught on a back pocket as well, as it could slide open if you press against the device while trying to cram the phone and keyboard into your pocket too quickly.

Despite the added heft, there is an advantage to the battery pack that powers the keyboard — it can provide wireless charging to products with MagSafe and Qi2. (You can opt to entirely disable wireless charging in the Clicks companion app, if you prefer to keep all the power reserved for the keyboard itself. Or you can designate a portion of the battery just for the keyboard.)

Another key advantage of the Power Keyboard is that it is highly customizable. Users can enable the Clicks key on the keyboard to function as a Tab button, or turn on “Cursor Mode” (Sym + CMD) to make certain letters on your keypad work as directional keys that move a cursor on the screen.

You can also adjust various settings like the idle timeout, battery reserves for wireless charging, LED backlight, and whether the Return key works as a hard or soft return. You can create your own Number Row shortcuts that allow you to press a number and the Sym button to enable Esc, volume controls, play/pause options, page up/down, and more.

And you can pair Apple Shortcuts with certain keys to do other things like start a call, get a weather forecast, turn on the flashlight, receive an AirDrop, send texts, and much more. (Several popular shortcuts are included in the Clicks app, but you can add your own.)

These, of course, are power user features that you’ll only appreciate if you get comfortable with typing on the keyboard first. That could take some time to learn, and arguably, you’ll be more comfortable using smaller, standard phones or lightweight options, like the iPhone Air. As for larger devices, we found it much easier to get started in landscape mode.

We also struggled to type comfortably with our iPhone case on, although it’s a heftier, protective case, not a slim case. To test the device, we removed the case and used our iPhone bare. While that was much better, it was still somewhat difficult to use because of the larger phone.

The company says it has tested the device with a number of phone models, including the iPhone Air, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max, 16 Pro, Pixel 9, Galaxy Fold, and other Android devices.

Whether the keyboard is worth the purchase has much to do with how much you really miss your BlackBerry; for the time being, it’s an affordable enough holdover until the company’s smartphone ships, at least. (Prototypes of the phone were much easier to use when we tried them at CES in January . It’s obviously easier to make a comfortable device when Clicks is in control of all the technical specifications, instead of having to create something that works with phones of various weights and sizes.)

While the Power Keyboard works as advertised, for the sake of comfort and portability, I’d prefer to make the switch to physical keys with Clicks’ Communicator smartphone.

If you also decide this keyboard is not for you, all is not lost: There’s still another way to use the product.

Because the Power Keyboard should be able to pair with any device that supports external Bluetooth keyboards, you could use it with tablets, smart TVs like the Apple TV, or AR/VR headsets, like the Apple Vision Pro. This could come in handy when you’re trying to set up new apps and have to type your email address and passwords awkwardly via a remote control or other input method.

TechCrunch tries new devices via review units, which are later returned to the company or donated, depending on the company’s specific return procedures.

articles.title: What comes after the smartphone? Amazon's Panos Panay will make his case at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026  | TechCrunch
articles.summary: At Disrupt 2026, Amazon's Panos Panay will provide his vision for what's in store for us beyond the smartphone.
articles.body:
For nearly 20 years, the smartphone has been at the center of hardware and software development. But with AI moving from stand-alone apps to being interwoven in our go-to platforms, and then into the operating system of our devices, the shape of the next generation of hardware devices is still being developed.

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , Amazon SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, Panos Panay will discuss how AI is changing the relationship between software, hardware, and the devices we use every day.

Disrupt has long been a place where the incumbents share where they’re placing their bets, and what impacts and opportunities startups need to know about. Your chance to get a jump-start on the competition starts October 13-15 at San Francisco’s Moscone West . Before we dig into Panay and his upcoming talk, you should consider locking in today’s ticket pricing before our next tier goes live . Our discounts won’t last much longer!

Why Panay brings a unique perspective to Disrupt 2026

Panay isn’t new to reinventing hardware categories under pressure. He spent more than 19 years at Microsoft, most notably working as their EVP and chief product officer, overseeing the development of a wide range of Surface devices, from to the original Surface Laptop from 2017 to the foldable Duo . While there, he also oversaw the development of Windows 11, in an overlap of software and hardware that’s becoming a mainstay in the AI era.

His departure from Microsoft was swiftly followed by the news he was joining Amazon , taking over from longtime consumer devices leader David Limp . Whereas Amazon had previously been very focused on the expansion of hardware through the home, Panay has been building around the generative AI revamp of Alexa, with the rollout of Alexa+ across several tiers of access in the U.S. earlier this year .

And at Disrupt, Panay will dive deeper into what’s coming up next for Amazon and Alexa+. As we potentially move into a world in which your daily routine doesn’t revolve around the phone in your hand, but on an assistant, a pair of glasses, or whatever form factor OpenAI is leaning into, the possibilities are endless! And that kind of future-forward thinking is available only at Disrupt .

articles.title: Apple could help you prove your iPhone photos aren’t deepfakes
articles.summary: iOS 27 beta 5 includes code references for an “Apple Reference Image” system that can embed provenance metadata into iPhone photographs.
articles.body: Apple is seemingly developing an iOS feature that can verify when a photograph was taken using an iPhone camera. 9to5Mac reports that the iOS 27 beta 5 includes code references for an “Apple Reference Image” system that can embed provenance metadata into iPhone photographs at the point of capture — enabling users to prove where the photo originated, and that it isn’t AI fakery. Apple Reference Image isn’t currently live, but a privacy disclosure in the iOS beta notes that the feature will be off by default. When (or if) it does roll out, 9to5Mac says it can be enabled via Settings > Camera > Reference Image > Reference Mode, and that only photographs taken using a new “Reference” option in the iPhone Camera app will include the provenance information required for authentication. MacRumors has more details about the actual authentication process, which doesn’t occur automatically and instead requires users to tap a Reference badge on the photograph. This reportedly sends the raw image and its embedded provenance data — including sensor signatures, capture time frame, and unique hardware identifiers — to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute servers for verification, and then returns the authenticated version with a uniquely assigned ID. [Image: This is the privacy disclosure that appears after Apple Reference Image has been enabled, according to 9to5Mac. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/reference-mode.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Apple doesn’t access the raw photo itself during this process, but it may receive sensor data that allows it to prevent images connected to compromised sensors from being authenticated, or retroactively revoke prior authentication on images associated with the sensor. Authenticated photos can be viewed on an iPhone, iPad, or Mac, according to MacRumors. By this description, Apple Reference Image works similarly to the C2PA Content Credentials provenance standard, which can be used to trace how and where an image was made, and if generative AI tools were used to make or manipulate it. Camera companies including Canon, Nikon, Sony, FujiFilm, and Leica have been gradually introducing it into their hardware, and Google’s Pixel 10 phone cameras also support the standard, but Apple has notably avoided adopting it. C2PA isn’t known for its reliability, however, so perhaps Apple believes its own system will be a better, more robust solution. Introducing a provenance system for iPhone photography also suggests Apple is throwing support behind labeling human-made works across online platforms — something Instagram head Adam Mosseri believes may be easier to achieve compared to identifying and labeling AI-generated content.

articles.title: Reservoir raises $8M to make water heaters that people — and the grid — will actually want | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Reservoir has built an ultra-efficient water heater that can predict hot water demand, store energy, and detect plumbing leaks throughout a home.
articles.body:
It’s hard to imagine a home appliance more forgotten — yet more consequential — than the water heater. Most people only think of water heaters when their shower runs cold, but they represent about 18% of a household’s total energy budget and are one of the main causes of residential water damage.

To Luke Winston-Almanzar, water heaters are in clear need of an upgrade. “The typical water heater is devoid of intelligence, it’s using a god-awful amount of energy, and my air fryer is smarter than it,” he told TechCrunch. “I was using more energy to heat my water than it takes to drive my electric car.”

So Winston-Almanzar, who was previously chief business officer at 3D-printing startup Formlabs , co-founded Reservoir along with Gabriel Parisi-Amon and Jake Felser to make a water heater that they would want to buy.

Reservoir announced Wednesday that it has raised $8 million in a seed round led by Asymmetric Capital Partners with participation from Founder Collective and MCJ.

The funding will help the company install more of its water heaters in homes around the Boston area, its initial market. Reservoir has installed about 100 devices to date, and Winston-Almanzar said his company hopes to have around 1,000 installed by the end of next year. “That’s when you start talking about a megawatt-scale in terms of capacity,” he said.

Storing megawatt-hours of energy as hot water could go a long way to stabilizing the grid. Today’s water heaters tend to be dumb devices, responding only to changes in temperature in the tank. But Reservoir, by predicting when people will need hot water, can heat the tank when electricity demand is low and prices are cheap. Plus, the device’s heat pump is nearly four times more efficient than an electric water heater and five times more efficient than a natural gas version.

The startup has been able to show that it can relieve strain on the grid at the neighborhood level, Winston-Almanzar said. Eventually, Reservoir could aggregate its fleet of water heaters to participate in utility demand response programs, which pay handsomely for large users to avoid tapping the grid at certain times. Winston-Almanzar said he’s looking at ways to use those payments to keep Reservoir’s prices down.

While energy storage might get grid experts excited, it won’t sell many water heaters. Most people replace their water heaters with whatever their plumber has on hand. The Reservoir team knew they needed to do more than build another heat pump water heater. “The sustainable product need to just be the better product,” he said.

To make an appliance that customers will seek out, Reservoir has included a number of features that aren’t found in typical water heaters.

The predictive heating feature ties in with energy storage. Reservoir’s water heater will spend the first month in a home gathering information about water usage patterns to train a model. Once trained, it will run the unit’s heat pump at the most efficient and cost-effective times to save money while also ensuring ample supply.

Reservoir also added an ultrasonic flow sensor to help detect plumbing leaks throughout the home, sending homeowners an alert through its app. In the Max version, Reservoir added more features, including a recirculation valve to provide instant hot water and a mixing valve that can prevent pipes from freezing in cold snaps. In the Max version, a 50-gallon tank can deliver up to 150 gallons of hot water in “party mode,” which can be set either on the device’s touchscreen or through the app.

To keep pricing simple and to speed up the sales process, Reservoir has also started its own plumbing company. Winston-Almanzar said that decision was inspired by his experience at Formlabs. “We built direct relationships [there] because, in a lot of cases, distributors weren’t embracing the new technology.”

Reservoir’s “Max” version costs $6,500, while the base “Core” version costs $5,000, installation costs included. Massachusetts residents qualify for a $1,050 rebate, bringing the price down significantly.

At $3,950, the Core model is competitive with or cheaper than existing heat pump water heaters. For comparison, the 80-gallon AO Smith that’s sitting in my basement currently costs about $3,500, and installation would add about $1,000. Traditional electric water heaters might cost less up front, at about $1,700 for an 80-gallon tank. But Winston-Almanzar said a Reservoir would save typical Boston homeowners up to $1,000 per year in energy costs. Breakeven should happen long before the Reservoir dies since the company offers a 10-year warranty.

“We don’t think it’s enough just to have great technology. We think it needs to be affordable,” Winston-Almanzar said.

Water heating is ripe for some new technology. The newest advance, heat pump water heaters, have failed to make a dent, commanding a small part of the market. If Reservoir succeeds, it might finally push them into the mainstream — and in the process take some pressure off the grid.

articles.title: Honor’s Robot Phone is better than a gimbal in a phone has any right to be
articles.summary: After an hour of testing the Robot Phone, I’m surprised but impressed.
articles.body: The Robot Phone, which launches today in China, doesn’t sound like a good idea — and not only because it’s not actually a robot. Instead it’s a regular Android smartphone with its main camera installed on a compact gimbal arm that unfolds from the phone’s rear. Cramming the equivalent of a DJI Osmo Pocket inside a smartphone sounds like a great way to get the worst of both worlds, but after an hour of testing, I’m cautiously optimistic that Honor has made this Frankenphone work.  This is a smaller gimbal than you’ll find on DJI’s compact Osmo Pocket line — Honor claims it’s the smallest in the world. It still makes the phone bulkier than normal, at 9.6mm thick (not counting the chunky camera section itself) and weighing 248g. Only the Samsung and Huawei trifolds are bigger, and my first impression was that the phone felt oddly dated as a result, despite the cutting-edge camera inside. The gimbal camera will spend most of its life tucked inside the phone’s camera module, protected by a small plastic screen. Even folded away, the 200-megapixel, 1/1.28-inch-type sensor serves as the phone’s main camera, joined by a 200-megapixel periscope telephoto and a 50-megapixel ultrawide.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/honor-robot-phone-01.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/honor-robot-phone-02.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/honor-robot-phone-03.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] But the real fun comes when the camera arm unfurls. First, you slide the plastic screen off — manually — so it covers the phone’s other two cameras instead. Then, activate the gimbal through the software, and it springs into action. (If you try to activate the gimbal without sliding away the cover, the phone won’t let you.)  During previous hands-off showcases, Honor has focused on the “Robot” part of the name, highlighting a cutesy chat interface powered by the company’s Yoyo AI assistant. The camera can nod or shake its “head,” dance to music, and make other expressive movements. It’s a cute gimmick, but little more, and I was relieved that in this briefing I was instead given the chance to put the camera to the test. Having the gimbal makes it easier to take selfies using the more powerful main camera, shoot at odd angles while keeping the display head-on, and record video with smooth panning and tracking. You control it using the phone’s default camera app, which offers simple controls in its photo and video tabs, and more complex options in a dedicated pro video section. Honor has also thrown in the fun option to take a panoramic selfie, the gimbal spinning around to take multiple photos and stitch them together.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/honor-robot-phone-07.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/honor-robot-phone-05.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/honor-robot-phone-06.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/honor-robot-phone-11.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The 3-axis gimbal has nearly 360 degrees of movement and a variety of tracking modes, including FPV, spin shot, super steady, and subject-tracking that can detect people as well as objects (and works in video calls too, though I’m not sure if anything beyond Weibo is supported). There are no additional physical controls, so you have to use an onscreen joystick for manual adjustments, which is a little finicky compared to dedicated hardware. Then again, the 6.3-inch phone screen is a much easier way to navigate settings and menus than an Osmo Pocket’s tiny display.  That’s helpful since Honor has packed in plenty of options. In addition to settings like resolution and frame rate, you can shoot in portrait or landscape, adjust the speed of the gimbal or the sensitivity of the joystick, switch aspect ratio, and toggle focus peaking on the display. Thanks to Honor’s partnership with camera company Arri, you can also record in a variety of different film-inspired looks, along with Arri’s own LogC3 format. [Image: Gimbal aside, this is a typical Android flagship from Honor. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/honor-robot-phone-08.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] An hour wasn’t enough time to fully assess the gimbal’s performance, but I did get a sense. Video felt a little less stable than I’m used to from this year’s Osmo Pocket 4, but not by much, which is impressive given how much smaller the setup is. A few minutes of sustained recording is enough to make the whole phone get pretty hot, but that’s true of DJI’s gimbal cameras too. I have a quick clip of test footage from my time with the phone, showing some simple panning from the main camera mode’s virtual joystick — I would have recorded something more exciting, but I wasn’t expecting to be allowed to publish the footage! [Media: https://youtu.be/EeVAxOZ-FdE] Photos seem to benefit from the gimbal too. The stabilization can help keep the camera steady between the multiple exposures that modern phones routinely stitch together for every photo you take. It was a bright, sunny day when I tested the phone, but when I stepped into a nearby church, it did an impressive job with the dimmer room and backlit stained glass windows. Between the fairly large sensor and the extra stabilization, this could be one of the better phones around for photos in dark conditions.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_20260729_145256.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_20260729_145533.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_20260729_145236.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_20260729_145227.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The other cameras seem impressive enough too, a natural fit for a phone that has flagship specs across the board. It’s powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, includes up to 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, and has a substantial 7,060mAh silicon-carbon battery. It probably needs it, given the extra power drain of the gimbal. The chunky, functional design language is the only real giveaway that this is anything other than a flagship slab phone, at least until that camera unfolds.  [Image: This is a thicker phone than most. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/honor-robot-phone-10.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Still, there are obvious reasons not to buy the Robot Phone. The first is that you probably can’t: Honor is only launching it in China, and has said it has no plans to release it elsewhere. That might change in a future iteration.  In China the phone starts from ¥9,999 (about $1,480). That’s ¥1,000 more than Honor’s Magic V6 foldable, which went on sale in the UK for £1,999.99 (about $2,700), which is a better reflection of how this is priced relative to other modern phones. That’s far more than simply buying a good phone and a separate Osmo Pocket, or the cheaper (if bulkier) option of a standalone gimbal to hold your phone. This is the classic foldable problem too (it’s like a phone plus a tablet for substantially more than the cost of both!). You’ll have to be willing to pay a real premium to combine those two gadgets into one. The benefits may be worth it for some, like livestreamers who want to be able to shoot stable smartphone video and stream it directly, but most people would likely be better served by separate products. The biggest concern is durability though. Honor says the phone has an IP54 rating for protection and dust and water when the camera is fully stowed, but that doesn’t apply when the gimbal is raised. Even closed, this is a little less tough than other flagship phones. That’s true of dedicated gimbal cameras too, but those aren’t likely to be exposed to potential damage nearly as often as your smartphone. Factor in the added risk of damage from drops, the potential for anything with moving parts to go wrong, and the presumably prohibitive cost of any repairs that fall outside Honor’s one-year warranty, and the Robot Phone is a big gamble for anyone to buy. [Image: The Yoyo AI chat mode includes cute animated eyes and fun animations. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/honor-robot-phone-12.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Do the tradeoffs make sense? For me, probably not. For some professional content creators, maybe.  I’m still not convinced it makes sense to squeeze a full gimbal arm inside a smartphone — Honor’s engineers were so preoccupied with whether or not they could, yadda yadda yadda — but this feels like just about the best version of the idea anyone could be expected to make. It’s bulky, and fragile, and fairly expensive. But it does things that no other phone camera can, and it mostly seems to do them well, while being a little better than most phones at selfies, and low light photos, and recording steady video. Just… don’t call it a robot, okay? Update, August 12th: Added pricing in China. Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title: Google unveils the Pixel Watch 5 with a smarter Gemini and advanced health monitoring | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The new smartwatch, which starts at $399, can track blood pressure patterns and insulin resistance, as well as deliver personalized help and better sleep tracking.
articles.body:
At its Made by Google event on Wednesday, Google unveiled the Pixel Watch 5 with a smarter Gemini experience, as well as advanced fitness and health monitoring. The new smartwatch, which starts at $399, can track blood pressure patterns and insulin resistance, as well as deliver personalized help and better sleep tracking.

Google says it designed the watch to deliver personalized and proactive help right when it’s needed. For example, the watch will proactively suggest relevant actions or information based on a text message’s context, like instantly pulling up a smoothie place your sister sent you.

You can raise your wrist to ask Gemini a question, handle requests like finding a nearby lunch spot with navigation, or use Gemini offline to manage timers, alarms, and workouts with your voice.

The watch will also dynamically surface timely updates right at the bottom of the watch face, like flight info, ETAs, and other helpful reminders.

The Pixel Watch 5 is also launching with “Health Guardian,” a suite of new proactive health and safety tools.

The tech giant says the smartwatch uses sensors and machine learning to track blood pressure patterns before they can put strain on your heart. Google says the feature was tested against 24-hour blood pressure monitors and uses an advanced waveform model trained on more than 1 billion minutes of data from over 500,000 people.

The insulin resistance feature is designed to identify changes in metabolic health that may be associated with insulin resistance and an increased risk of developing prediabetes or type 2 diabetes. The feature combines signals from sleep, heart rate, physical activity, and other health data. A large sensor model then analyzes these signals over time to identify long-term changes in insulin resistance.

Google will give users a summary of their blood pressure and insulin resistance trends every month.

There’s also a new feature that can detect a persistent drop in oxygen saturation and will contact emergency services if the watch determines that a breathing emergency may be occurring. This feature is launching in select European countries before expanding to additional regions.

Additionally, the watch’s sleep-stage tracking is 15% more accurate, and there’s also a new bedtime watch face that reduces nighttime distractions. A new “Smart Wake” feature wakes users at an optimal point in their sleep cycle, while a new sleep breathing quality metric tracks minute-by-minute changes in blood oxygen levels.

As for fitness, Google says the Pixel Watch 5 delivers its most accurate GPS route tracking yet, with route mapping that’s two times more accurate than previous generations. The improved accuracy is designed to provide users with more precise workout and running data, including a closer match between your recorded route and the actual course.

The Pixel Watch 5 features the Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 platform and has 12% more CPU performance and 50% more RAM than the previous platform. Google says the Watch 5 is 20% faster overall.

The Pixel Watch 5 supports up to 40 hours of battery life and is available in new colors, including Canyon Fog and Olive. The 41mm version starts at $399, while the 44mm starts at $429. The smartwatch is available for preorder starting Wednesday and will be available on August 20.
